item.title: Oracle Launches AI Development Resources for RAG, Agents, and Database Integration
item.description:
Oracle Launches AI Development Resources for RAG, Agents, and Database Integration

Oracle has released a suite of technical resources to help developers build AI applications, agents, and systems using Oracle AI Database and OCI services. These materials include reference apps, notebooks, and workshops covering RAG, vector and hybrid search, AI agents, and agent memory, with practical examples using LangChain and LangGraph. The repository provides complete, working examples that showcase end-to-end implementations, including source code, deployment configurations, and documentation for understanding architectural patterns and best practices.

📚 Available Resources

  • Reference apps, notebooks, and workshops for RAG, vector and hybrid search, AI agents, and agent memory
  • Integration examples using LangChain and LangGraph
  • Applications demonstrating AI-powered solutions with Oracle technologies
  • Complete, working end-to-end implementations with source code and deployment configs

🧪 Featured Implementations

Application Description
Gamified fitness platform Built with Oracle 26ai JSON Duality Views (FastAPI + Redis), created live during a webinar
Intelligent RAG system Multi-agent Chain of Thought (CoT), PDF/Web/Repo processing, with Oracle AI Database 26ai integration
Financial services AI agent Uses Oracle AI Database as a unified memory core for vector, graph, spatial, and relational queries
Next.js chatbot Pairs Oracle AI Database 26ai SQL, vector, and hybrid search with typed generative UI components
Full-stack AI application Oracle JET UI, OCI Generative AI integration, Kubernetes deployment, and Terraform infrastructure
AI chat app Uses TanStack Start and Oracle 26ai Select AI to query a shoe store database with natural language
Team knowledge base Slack, GitHub and docs connectors; in-database ONNX embeddings; Oracle Text + vector hybrid retrieval with RRF through langchain-oracledb; per-caller access control via DBMS_RLS row policy; exposed to Claude Code over MCP and LangChain create_agent CLI
AI agent harness Migrates RAG corpus from MongoDB into Oracle AI Database 26ai while preserving vector search and enabling SQL/JSON Duality queries

🔧 Key Technologies

  • Oracle AI Database 26ai with JSON Duality Views
  • Vector and hybrid search capabilities
  • langchain-oracledb for integration
  • DBMS_RLS for row-level security and access control
  • ONNX embeddings processed in-database
  • Support for LangChain and LangGraph frameworks
  • OCI Generative AI service integration
  • Kubernetes and Terraform for deployment

#OracleAI #RAG #LangChain #VectorDatabase #AIAgents #LangGraph

Source: oracle-devrel/oracle-ai-developer-hub

item.title: Lakebase Postgres Introduces Read Replicas with Decoupled Compute and Storage
item.description:
Lakebase Postgres Introduces Read Replicas with Decoupled Compute and Storage

Lakebase Postgres has introduced a new approach to read replicas that decouples compute from storage, enabling faster scaling and lower costs compared to traditional managed PostgreSQL services like Amazon RDS.

🔍 Overview

The traditional read replica model faces significant challenges when scaling reads on demand. In managed Postgres services, a replica is a physical clone of the primary: its own instance, storage volume, and full copy of every page. This makes replicas impractical for elastic scaling because they take minutes to hours to create, each adds a full data copy to billing, and they run continuously even after traffic spikes subside.

🧩 How it Works

Lakebase Postgres separates compute from storage. In traditional systems, Postgres runs on a single machine owning both execution and durable state. Lakebase splits these responsibilities: since compute owns nothing durable, multiple compute instances can attach to the same storage. A read replica is simply an independent, read-only compute that reads from the shared storage. Creating one requires no data copy, no replication work on the primary (which continues streaming WAL to safekeepers), and no dependency on database size—resulting in seconds-long creation times regardless of scale.

⚙️ Key Details

  • In traditional setups, N replicas mean N+1 copies of the database (one on primary, one per replica volume)
  • In Lakebase Postgres, N replicas still mean one storage copy
  • Replicas maintain only local caches (shared buffers and NVMe), not durable data
  • Storage is billed solely for the data in the storage layer; replicas add compute, not storage
  • Replica costs follow the reads they serve, not database size or hourly instance billing

💡 Why It Matters

The monolithic implementation of replicas in systems like Amazon RDS creates the opposite of their intended purpose. Instead of elastic scaling, you get static, overprovisioned infrastructure. Lakebase’s decoupled architecture fixes both creation time and cost inefficiencies by treating replicas as lightweight compute instances rather than full database clones.

#PostgreSQL #Database #Scalability #Lakebase #ComputeStorageDecoupling

Source: Rethinking read replicas for the lakebase architecture

item.title: Flexible GraphRAG v0.11.0 Release Introduces New Desktop App and State Options
item.description:
Flexible GraphRAG v0.11.0 Release Introduces New Desktop App and State Options

The v0.11.0 release introduces an early version of a Desktop App built with Tauri and Rust alongside various backend and architectural updates.

🚀 Availability

  • New v0.11.0 release on 11/16/26.
  • Includes an early version of a Desktop App (Tauri/Rust) around the React, Vue, or Angular UI with 5 Flexible GraphRAG tabs.
  • Adds browsing, ingesting, searching, and graph viewing (5th tab) of local files and folders with auto-sync support.

⚙️ Key details

  • The backend is written in Python, utilizing LlamaIndex and LangChain as peer frameworks.
  • LlamaIndex serves as the default for each pipeline stage, while LangChain can be selected per stage via environment configuration.
  • The API is built as a REST FastAPI service.
  • Frontend options include Angular, React, and Vue TypeScript frontends, alongside an included MCP server.
  • An optional lighter Docker-free configuration uses SQLite as the auto-sync incremental update state store (INCREMENTAL_STATE_STORE=sqlite) along with embedded stores such as LanceDB, BM25, and LadybugDB.
  • Databases and dashboards can be enabled using the provided Docker Compose layout.

🧩 Capabilities and Integrations

  • Supports 14 data sources (10 with incremental auto-sync).
  • Supports 15 property graph databases, 4 RDF triple stores, 10 vector databases, OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, BM25 search, Alfresco, and Nuxeo.
  • File and folder browser available via Browse… in the Alfresco, Nuxeo, CMIS, SharePoint, OneDrive, Box, S3, Azure Blob, GCS, and Google Drive data source forms for both desktop and web UIs.
  • Optional ingest pipeline, hybrid search, and AI query can run through customizable Langflow visual flows utilizing 12 custom Langflow components.
  • Optional ingest can run on a CocoIndex (Rust engine) pipeline reusing the same sources, targets, parsers, and KG extractors, adding step-level memoization and automatic delete reconciliation.
  • Optional integration with Hyland OpenArch as a search and vector store, as well as a store for data sources and document state.

#GraphRAG #Python #Tauri #LlamaIndex #FastAPI

Source: stevereiner/flexible-graphrag

item.title: Lakebase Postgres minimizes object‑storage reads using tiered caching
item.description:
Lakebase Postgres minimizes object‑storage reads using tiered caching

Lakebase Postgres builds on object storage for durability while keeping reads off of it through a multi‑tier cache hierarchy.

🔍 Overview

  • Object storage provides the foundation: durable, bottomless storage, instant branches and restores, and a single copy of data for transactions and analytics (LTAP).
  • The system is designed so that object storage never sits in front of a query; reads travel through faster tiers first.

🧩 Architecture

Tier Role
Compute node Runs standard Postgres, holds no durable state, serves ~99.46% of page accesses from its local cache (memory or micro‑second latency).
Pageserver Owns local NVMe, serves ~0.54% of reads, builds an LSM tree, persists materialized history to object storage asynchronously.
Object storage Holds immutable, long‑term history, backs pageservers, is accessed for only ~1 in 28 million page accesses.

⚙️ Read Path Details

  • On a compute‑node cache miss, the request is sent over the network to a pageserver, which serves the page from its own NVMe.
  • Only if the pageserver also misses does the request reach object storage.
  • Production statistics:
    • Compute cache: ~1.1 billion page accesses / s (99.46% of total).
    • Pageserver NVMe: ~6 million reads / s (0.54% of total).
    • Object storage: ~39 requests / s (≈1 in 28 million accesses).
  • Reads that do reach object storage are rare one‑offs—old branches, restores, or databases that have been idle for weeks. Once cached, subsequent reads return to the faster tiers.

🚀 Availability & Durability

  • Transactions are committed after a quorum of safekeepers acknowledges the record.
  • A Paxos‑based protocol handles leader election and failover.
  • Because the compute layer holds no durable state, it can start, stop, scale, or fail without risking data.
  • The storage layer owns correctness, durability, and history.

💡 Why it matters

  • By keeping the hot path in memory or NVMe, Lakebase Postgres achieves micro‑second latency comparable to a traditional warm‑cache Postgres instance.
  • Object storage provides virtually unlimited capacity and durability without becoming a performance bottleneck.
  • The tiered design ensures that even as data grows, the vast majority of reads stay on the fastest tier, making the system both scalable and responsive.

#Lakebase #Postgres #ObjectStorage #DatabaseArchitecture

Source: Built on object storage, served from cache

item.title: ARCS Benchmark Highlights Ambiguity Challenges in Text-to-SQL
item.description:
ARCS Benchmark Highlights Ambiguity Challenges in Text-to-SQL

On 7 Oct 2026, researchers submitted a paper titled “ARCS: Towards Precise Text-to-SQL via Structured Disambiguation” to the Computer Science > Computation and Language category on arXiv.

🔍 Overview

  • Text‑to‑SQL systems encounter errors primarily due to ambiguity in user questions.
  • Ambiguities are often subtle, domain‑specific, and can silently shift outputs away from the user’s intent.
  • Traditional conversational clarification is inefficient, cognitively demanding, and misaligned with real‑world workflows.

🧩 Problem: Ambiguity in Text-to-SQL

  • Ambiguities arise naturally in real‑world databases.
  • They are difficult to detect without explicit signals.
  • Existing dialogue‑based fixes add overhead for users.

⚙️ Proposed Solution: Structured Disambiguation

  • Introduces a new paradigm where ambiguity is resolved through explicit, constrained interactions rather than free‑form dialogue.
  • Emphasizes precise, limited exchanges that directly target the ambiguous element.

📊 Benchmark: ARCS Corpus

  • ARCS (Ambiguity Resolution Corpus for SQL) is the first text‑to‑SQL benchmark that:
    • Contains naturally occurring, unconstrained ambiguities over real‑world databases. - Provides complete annotations of every valid ambiguity point, possible interpretations, and the corresponding SQL queries.

📈 Results

Model End‑to‑End Execution Accuracy
gpt-6-sol 51%
Open‑source models ≤27%
  • The results show that even state‑of‑the‑art models struggle when ambiguity is present.

💡 Why it matters

  • Highlights the need for better ambiguity handling before large‑scale deployment.
  • Offers a public resource (ARCS) for researchers to develop and evaluate structured disambiguation methods.
  • Sets a baseline that reveals a substantial performance gap for open‑source systems.

#TextToSQL #StructuredDisambiguation #Benchmark

Source: ARCS: Towards Precise Text-to-SQL via Structured Disambiguation
